script.opening: "Hello doctor. I’ve got this ulcer in my mouth, on the side of my tongue, been there about six weeks. I’m sure it’s just my denture rubbing — it catches there. The wife wanted me to ring because it’s not gone. Could you just prescribe one of those mouth gels or a mouthwash for ulcers? I’ve got a photo. Oh, and there’s a bit of a lump come up in my neck but that’s probably a gland from the ulcer, isn’t it."

facts.text: If characterised (history + photo): an ulcer present >3 WEEKS (≈6 weeks), NOT healing, with RAISED/FIRM (indurated) edges, occasional bleeding, on a high-risk site (lateral tongue/floor of mouth) — plus a NECK LUMP (possible lymphadenopathy). NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer with unexplained ulceration in the oral cavity lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent and unexplained neck lump; the indurated, persistent, bleeding ulcer with a neck node is high concern, so referral is clearly warranted.

On questioning: 40-year smoker, daily alcohol, and BETEL/PAAN (areca nut) chewing — all major risk factors for oral squamous cell carcinoma (and tobacco+alcohol synergise; betel is independently carcinogenic). High-risk profile.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just the denture rubbing" is fear-driven denial: his brother had mouth/throat cancer and a hard time with treatment, and Frank is frightened of the same — the disfigurement, the treatment, dying like his brother — so he’s reframed it as a benign denture sore and is pushing for a gel to avoid facing it. There may also be cultural reluctance/shame around the betel chewing he’s downplaying.

A rubbing denture CAN cause ulcers — but a denture ulcer should heal within ~2–3 weeks once the cause is removed/adjusted; a non-healing, indurated ulcer with a neck node cannot be explained away by the denture, and assuming so is the trap.

Officially: a mouth gel/mouthwash to soothe the ulcer. What he needs: recognition that an unexplained, non-healing oral ulcer >3 weeks (with induration and a neck node, in a high-risk patient) warrants an oral cancer suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12) and examination — with his fear and the betel/alcohol/smoking addressed sensitively.

ice.ideas: It’s just an ulcer from his denture rubbing; a gel or mouthwash will sort it; the neck lump is just a gland.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his brother had mouth/throat cancer and suffered; Frank is frightened of the same and has reframed it as a denture sore to avoid facing it; possible cultural shame about betel chewing.
ice.expectations: A mouth gel/mouthwash. What he actually needs: examination and an urgent oral cancer suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-healing indurated ulcer + neck node, with his fear and risk factors addressed.

cues: Non-healing ulcer >3 weeks + firm/raised edges + bleeding + neck lump on a high-risk site — oral cancer suspected cancer pathway, not a denture sore.
Smoker + daily alcohol + betel/paan — stacked oral-cancer risk factors.
"Just the denture, the lump’s probably a gland" — denial; brother’s cancer is the fear underneath.

checkpoints.text: Recognises an UNEXPLAINED oral ulcer persisting >3 WEEKS (non-healing, indurated/firm edges, bleeding, high-risk site) as suspicious for oral cancer, and does NOT accept the "denture rubbing" explanation or prescribe a gel and wait

Acts on the NICE NG12 pathway: makes the suspected cancer pathway referral that NG12 says to consider for oral cancer with unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks or a persistent unexplained neck lump — and notes that at 63 the neck lump also meets the NG12 laryngeal criterion (age 45 and over with an unexplained neck lump or persistent hoarseness); restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12 — and knows the NG12 urgent dentist route is for a lump on the lip or in the mouth, or red or red-and-white patches

Takes the NECK LUMP seriously: a persistent unexplained neck lump is itself a NICE NG12 criterion (oral cancer; and laryngeal cancer at 45 and over) and, with the ulcer, raises concern for nodal spread — not simply "a reactive gland"
Examines properly (in person, not just the photo): inspects and PALPATES the lesion (induration) and the neck nodes, checks the whole oral cavity, rather than relying on a video impression

Elicits and weights the risk factors (smoking, alcohol, betel/areca-nut/paan) and addresses them — recognising betel as an independent carcinogen — and recognises the denture as a distractor (a denture ulcer should heal in ~2–3 weeks once adjusted)

Hears the denial as fear, surfaces the brother’s cancer gently, and treats the wife’s prompting as the reliable signal rather than colluding with "just the denture"; handles betel-chewing without cultural judgement
Balances honesty with reassurance (many mouth ulcers are benign, but a non-healing one needs urgent checking), and addresses the fear of treatment/disfigurement with compassion

Safety-nets and follows up: explains the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral) and what to expect (specialist examination, likely biopsy), what would warrant sooner review, smoking/alcohol/betel cessation support, ensures he attends, documents, and tracks the result

worked.txt: "I’m really glad your wife got you to ring. I’m not going to just send a gel, though, and I’ll tell you why honestly. A denture rub does cause ulcers — but those heal within a couple of weeks once we ease the denture. An ulcer that’s been there six weeks, isn’t healing, has firm raised edges and bleeds, especially with a lump in the neck — that’s a different situation and we have to check it properly."

"I need to see and feel it in person, not just on a photo — I’ll look at the whole mouth, feel the ulcer itself, and feel that lump in your neck. A photo’s a start, but feeling whether something’s firm is exactly the bit that matters here. The neck lump isn’t something I want to write off as ‘just a gland’ either."

"Based on this, you meet the criteria for an urgent referral to the mouth/throat specialists — seen quickly, aiming for an answer within 28 days — who’ll examine you and almost certainly take a small sample. That’s what the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, says to consider for a mouth ulcer that hasn’t healed in three weeks, and even more so with the neck lump. It is NOT me saying it’s cancer; it’s making sure, quickly."

"Can I gently ask — is there a reason this has worried you more than you’re letting on? … Your brother, and what he went through. I’m so sorry. That makes total sense of wanting it to be just the denture. But that fear is exactly why we look now, early — because if anything IS there, catching it early changes everything about how treatable and how manageable it is."

"You mentioned smoking, a daily drink, and the paan. No judgement — but those together are the main things that irritate the mouth lining, and the betel especially. Stopping or cutting down really matters now, and I’ll help you with all of it, gently, whenever you’re ready. Today’s priority is getting you seen."

"So: I’ll examine you and get the urgent referral in today. If it bleeds a lot, you struggle to swallow or speak, or the lump grows, come back sooner. I’ll note exactly how things look and follow up the result with you. You came in for a gel; what I’m doing is making sure that if there’s something to find, we find it early — that’s what gives you the best outcome."

f.learning: An unexplained oral ulcer persisting >3 weeks — non-healing, with indurated (firm/raised) edges and bleeding, on a high-risk site — is suspicious for oral cancer and must not be reassured away as a "denture rub" (a denture ulcer should heal within ~2–3 weeks once the cause is adjusted). The NICE NG12 action is to consider an oral cancer suspected cancer pathway referral for ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks — and with these features, to make it — and a persistent unexplained neck lump is itself an NG12 criterion (oral cancer, and laryngeal cancer at 45 and over) — with the ulcer it raises concern for nodal spread, not "just a gland". Examine and PALPATE in person (induration, neck nodes) rather than relying on a photo, and weight the risk factors — smoking, alcohol (which synergise) and betel/areca-nut/paan (an independent carcinogen). The examinable hidden agenda is fear-driven denial: a brother who had head-and-neck cancer, with dread of treatment/disfigurement, reframed as a benign denture sore, plus possible cultural reluctance around betel. Surface the fear, treat the wife’s prompting as the reliable signal, address risk factors without cultural judgement, balance honesty with reassurance, and complete the suspected cancer pathway referral with documentation and follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG209 Tobacco (2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE PH24 Alcohol-use disorders: prevention (2010)
knowledge.summary: An unexplained mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent unexplained neck lump, meets the NICE NG12 threshold for a suspected cancer pathway referral. A denture does not explain a 6-week, firm, bleeding ulcer with a neck lump.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer in people with unexplained ulceration in the oral cavity lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent and unexplained lump in the neck. Frank has both.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained lump in the neck. At 63 with a neck lump, he meets this as well; the head and neck team covers both.

NICE NG12: consider urgent referral for assessment by a dentist for a lump on the lip or in the oral cavity, or a red or red-and-white patch consistent with erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia. The dentist is a route for patches and lumps, not a substitute for the suspected cancer pathway when the ulcer criterion is met.

Denture trauma causes ulcers, but they heal once the denture is eased. Features that make trauma an unsafe explanation: more than 3 weeks, raised firm (indurated) edges, bleeding, lateral tongue or floor of mouth, and a neck lump.

Tobacco and alcohol are the main risk factors and multiply each other’s effect. Areca nut (in betel quid and paan) is classed as a human carcinogen by IARC (international). Offer stop smoking support (NICE NG209) and alcohol brief advice (NICE PH24).
The specialist will examine, usually biopsy the ulcer, and may scan the neck. NHS England’s Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

dg.d: Open question about the ulcer; takes the neck lump seriously as part of the agenda rather than a throwaway.
Smoking, daily alcohol and paan asked without judgement; the wife’s role; his brother’s illness.
Arranges face-to-face examination to palpate the ulcer and neck; explains the specialist will examine and biopsy.
Denture trauma versus oral cancer; checks whether easing the denture has helped and whether the lump persists.
Duration over 3 weeks, induration, bleeding, neck lump; asks about swallowing, voice, ear pain and weight loss.
States that the ulcer is suspicious and meets the NICE NG12 criteria, without claiming it is cancer.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer sent today (NICE NG12); gel for comfort only.
Offers stop smoking support, alcohol advice and paan cessation respectfully; denture left out meanwhile.
Chase if no contact within a week; same-day contact for heavy bleeding, swallowing or breathing trouble; results reviewed together.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: The wife’s worry and “that’s just a gland, isn’t it?” are followed up and lead to the fear underneath.
Idea (denture sore); concern (brother’s mouth and throat cancer, fear of treatment); expectation (gel or mouthwash).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his brother had mouth/throat cancer and suffered; Frank is frightened of the same and has reframed it as a denture sore to avoid facing it; possible cultural shame about betel chewing — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Mensah, I’m Dr Shah. Can you hear and see me clearly? Thanks for sending the photo. Tell me about the ulcer in your own words.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens with the patient’s story

model.text: It’s on the side of my tongue, been there about six weeks. It’s the denture rubbing, I’m sure. The wife made me ring. Can you just give me a gel or a mouthwash? Oh, and there’s a bit of a lump in my neck, but that’s a gland from the ulcer, isn’t it?
I’m glad your wife encouraged you. I’d like to understand the ulcer properly and have a think about the lump too, then we’ll agree what to do. Is that alright?
model.why: Sets an agenda that includes both problems he raised

model.text: Fine.
Has it changed at all over the six weeks? Does it bleed, and how does the edge feel with your tongue?
model.why: Characterises duration, change, bleeding and induration

model.text: It’s not getting better. The edges feel a bit raised and hard now. It bleeds sometimes when I eat.
Have you tried leaving the denture out, or had it adjusted? And has the lump in your neck gone down at all?
model.why: Tests the denture hypothesis and the persistence of the neck lump

model.text: I leave it out at night. Still there. The lump’s about the same, maybe a bit bigger.
Any trouble swallowing or speaking, a change in your voice, ear pain, or weight loss?
model.why: Screens for other head and neck red flags

model.text: No, none of that really.
Can I ask about a few everyday things? Do you smoke, how much do you usually drink, and do you ever chew betel, paan or areca nut? I ask everyone with a mouth problem.
model.why: Elicits all three risk factors without judgement, normalising the question

model.text: I smoke, forty years now. A drink every day. And the paan, now and then. It’s just what we grew up with.
Thank you for being straight with me, that’s helpful.
model.why: Acknowledges an honest disclosure without shaming

model.text: You’ve said it’s the denture, but it sounds like your wife is worried. Is there anything that’s been on your mind about it yourself?
model.why: Uses the wife’s concern as a cue to explore his own fear

model.text: …My brother had cancer of the mouth, the throat. He had a terrible time with the treatment. I don’t want to go through that. So I’d rather it was the denture.
I’m so sorry about your brother. After seeing what he went through, of course you’d want this to be something simple. Thank you for telling me, it helps me understand.
model.why: Names and validates the fear driving the denial

model.text: I want to be honest with you. A denture sore should heal within a few weeks once it’s eased. An ulcer that’s been there six weeks, with firm edges, that bleeds, together with a lump in the neck, can’t safely be put down to the denture.
model.why: Explains why the denture explanation is unsafe

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I can’t tell that from here, and most mouth ulcers aren’t cancer. But national guidance says an ulcer that hasn’t healed after three weeks, or a lump in the neck that stays, should be seen quickly by the head and neck specialists, within two weeks. You have both, so that’s what I recommend.
model.why: Applies the NICE NG12 criteria honestly without over-stating the diagnosis

model.text: What will they do?

They’ll look and feel carefully, and most likely take a small sample from the ulcer under local anaesthetic. That gives a definite answer. If there is something there, finding it early is what makes treatment smaller and more successful.
model.why: Sets expectations and links early diagnosis to his fear of treatment

model.text: I’d also like to see you in the surgery in the next day or two, so I can feel the ulcer and the neck myself. A photo can’t show me how firm it is. I’ll send the referral today either way. Does that work?
model.why: Arranges a face-to-face examination without delaying the referral

model.text: Yes, I can come in. What about the gel?
If it’s sore, a pharmacy anaesthetic gel or mouthwash is fine for comfort, but it won’t replace being seen. Keep the denture out as much as you can for now.
model.why: Meets his request safely without letting it become the plan

model.text: The smoking, the daily drink and the paan all affect the lining of the mouth. I’m not going to lecture you today. When you’re ready, there’s good help to stop smoking and to cut down, and I’d be glad to set it up. Would you like that?
model.why: Offers risk-factor support respectfully and lets him choose

model.text: Maybe the smoking. Let me get this sorted first.

That’s fair. The hospital should contact you within days. If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If it bleeds heavily, you struggle to swallow or breathe, or the neck lump grows quickly, contact us the same day.
model.why: Specific safety-net and responsibility for chasing the referral

model.text: Would it help if your wife came with you to the appointment? And can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
Urgent referral to the mouth and throat people, come in to see you this week, gel just for comfort, ring if I don’t hear in a week. She’ll come with me.
Exactly right. I know this isn’t what you rang for, and it took courage to tell me about your brother. We’ll go through the results together.
model.why: Acknowledges the shift from his request and commits to continuity

social.t: Betel, paan and areca nut chewing can be a long-standing social and cultural habit. Ask about it routinely and neutrally; many patients do not know it carries a cancer risk.
His brother’s difficult treatment drives his avoidance. His wife is an ally in getting him to appointments.

legal.t: Explain why a suspected cancer referral is being made, what it involves and that it does not mean cancer is confirmed. Patients who are told the reason are more likely to attend.

professional.t: The GP remains responsible for checking the patient is seen. Record the referral, the reason given to the patient and a plan to follow up if he does not hear.
A photo cannot show induration or feel the neck. Arrange examination in person, but do not delay the referral waiting for it.

community.t: NHS Stop Smoking Services; local alcohol support; Macmillan Cancer Support and the Mouth Cancer Foundation for information while he waits.

redFlags: Unexplained oral ulceration for more than 3 weeks: suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer (NICE NG12)
Persistent unexplained neck lump: oral cancer criterion, and laryngeal criterion at 45 and over
Raised, firm edges, bleeding, lateral tongue site; difficulty swallowing, voice change, ear pain, weight loss
psychosocial: Forty years of smoking, daily alcohol and occasional paan
Brother’s head and neck cancer and his experience of treatment
His wife’s concern as a reliable signal
ice: Idea: “It’s the denture rubbing; the lump is just a gland”
Concern: ending up like his brother
Expectation: a mouth gel or mouthwash

playbook.diagnosis: “This ulcer has been there six weeks, has firm edges and bleeds, and there’s a lump in your neck. That doesn’t fit with a denture sore, so it needs checking quickly by the head and neck specialists.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A sore from a denture is like a blister from new shoes: once the rubbing stops, it heals. This one hasn’t healed even with the denture out, so we need someone to take a proper look and probably a small sample.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me about your brother, and I understand why you’d want this to be the denture. Getting it checked early is the best way to avoid what he went through.”
management.psychosocial: Respect his pace on smoking, drinking and paan: make one open offer of support and let him choose. Involve his wife if he wants.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to head and neck today (NICE NG12)
Face-to-face examination this week to palpate the ulcer and neck, without delaying the referral
Gel for comfort only; denture out where possible; stop smoking support offered
safetyNet: Ring if no hospital contact within a week
Same-day contact for heavy bleeding, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a rapidly growing lump

pitfalls.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on knowledge of NICE NG12. They fail by going along with the patient’s explanation, missing the neck lump, or losing him with a lecture. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Prescribes a gel and asks him to return in two weeks if it hasn’t healed.
items.why: The ulcer has already lasted six weeks. It meets the NICE NG12 threshold now. “Management not in line with UK guidance.”
items.fix: State the criterion plainly and send the suspected cancer pathway referral today.

items.fail: Accepts “the lump is just a gland from the ulcer”.
items.why: A persistent unexplained neck lump is its own NICE NG12 criterion, and with the ulcer raises concern for spread.
items.fix: Ask how long it has been there and whether it is changing, and include it in the referral.

items.why: Induration and nodes are felt, not seen. Over-reliance on a remote image is unsafe.
items.fix: Refer now and arrange a face-to-face examination this week; one does not wait for the other.

items.fail: Lectures on smoking, drinking and paan before he feels heard.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s perspective.” Shame about a cultural habit can end engagement.
items.fix: Ask neutrally, thank him for honesty, and make one open offer of support later in the consultation.

items.fail: Never discovers why he wants it to be the denture.
items.why: “Did not explore concerns.” His brother’s cancer is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Use the wife’s worry: “It sounds like she’s worried. What about you?”

items.fail: Says “it’s probably cancer” or, conversely, “I’m sure it’s nothing”.
items.why: Both are poorly calibrated communication and damage trust.
items.fix: “Most mouth ulcers aren’t cancer, but this one needs a proper look, quickly.”

timeMap.d: He mentions the neck lump at the end of his opening. Put it on the agenda straight away.
Six weeks, raised firm edges, bleeding, denture out without improvement, persistent lump. Smoking, alcohol and paan asked neutrally.
Use the wife’s worry to open the door. His brother’s cancer surfaces; acknowledge it before any explanation.
Why not the denture. NICE NG12 criteria in plain words. Suspected cancer pathway referral today; face-to-face examination this week.
Offer stop smoking help without lecturing. Chase if no contact in a week. Same-day symptoms. Teach-back; offer for his wife to come.

wordPics.fail: Accepts the denture story and prescribes a gel; dismisses the neck lump as a gland; no suspected cancer pathway referral; relies on the photo; never asks about smoking, alcohol or paan, or lectures about them; never learns about the brother.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the ulcer and neck lump as NICE NG12 criteria and refers on the suspected cancer pathway; asks about risk factors; arranges examination; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus surfaces the brother’s cancer and uses it to frame early referral as protective, explains honestly without over-stating, handles paan with cultural respect, meets the gel request safely, takes ownership of chasing the referral and checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably the denture. Try this gel and come back if it isn’t better in a couple of weeks.”
avoid.instead: “A denture sore should have healed by now. Six weeks with firm edges and a neck lump needs the specialists to see you within two weeks.”
avoid.why: A further wait with a gel is the classic missed-cancer error in this station.

avoid.dont: “You really must stop smoking, drinking and chewing that stuff — it causes cancer.”
avoid.instead: “These things affect the mouth lining. When you’re ready, I’d be glad to help you cut down or stop.”
avoid.why: A shaming lecture at a frightening moment loses the patient; an open offer keeps him engaged.

avoid.instead: “I’m asking the specialists to check this quickly. Most mouth ulcers aren’t cancer, but this one needs a proper look.”
avoid.why: Honest but calibrated language respects his fear without false reassurance.

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I can’t tell that from here, and most mouth ulcers aren’t cancer. But national guidance says an ulcer that hasn’t healed after three weeks, or a lump in the neck that stays, should be seen quickly by the head and neck specialists, within two weeks. You have both, so that’s what I recommend.
SCA_MODELS.why: Applies the NICE NG12 criteria honestly without over-stating the diagnosis

SCA_MODELS.text: What will they do?

They’ll look and feel carefully, and most likely take a small sample from the ulcer under local anaesthetic. That gives a definite answer. If there is something there, finding it early is what makes treatment smaller and more successful.
SCA_MODELS.why: Sets expectations and links early diagnosis to his fear of treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d also like to see you in the surgery in the next day or two, so I can feel the ulcer and the neck myself. A photo can’t show me how firm it is. I’ll send the referral today either way. Does that work?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges a face-to-face examination without delaying the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I can come in. What about the gel?
If it’s sore, a pharmacy anaesthetic gel or mouthwash is fine for comfort, but it won’t replace being seen. Keep the denture out as much as you can for now.
SCA_MODELS.why: Meets his request safely without letting it become the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: The smoking, the daily drink and the paan all affect the lining of the mouth. I’m not going to lecture you today. When you’re ready, there’s good help to stop smoking and to cut down, and I’d be glad to set it up. Would you like that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers risk-factor support respectfully and lets him choose

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe the smoking. Let me get this sorted first.

That’s fair. The hospital should contact you within days. If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If it bleeds heavily, you struggle to swallow or breathe, or the neck lump grows quickly, contact us the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and responsibility for chasing the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Would it help if your wife came with you to the appointment? And can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
Urgent referral to the mouth and throat people, come in to see you this week, gel just for comfort, ring if I don’t hear in a week. She’ll come with me.
Exactly right. I know this isn’t what you rang for, and it took courage to tell me about your brother. We’ll go through the results together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the shift from his request and commits to continuity

SCA_STEM.name: Frank Mensah
SCA_STEM.recent: Retired bus driver. No consultations in the past year. Has sent a photo of a sore area inside his mouth ahead of the call.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about a mouth ulcer that has not healed.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG209 Tobacco (2021) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE PH24 Alcohol-use disorders: prevention (2010)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An unexplained mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent unexplained neck lump, meets the NICE NG12 threshold for a suspected cancer pathway referral. A denture does not explain a 6-week, firm, bleeding ulcer with a neck lump.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer in people with unexplained ulceration in the oral cavity lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent and unexplained lump in the neck. Frank has both.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained lump in the neck. At 63 with a neck lump, he meets this as well; the head and neck team covers both.

NICE NG12: consider urgent referral for assessment by a dentist for a lump on the lip or in the oral cavity, or a red or red-and-white patch consistent with erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia. The dentist is a route for patches and lumps, not a substitute for the suspected cancer pathway when the ulcer criterion is met.

Denture trauma causes ulcers, but they heal once the denture is eased. Features that make trauma an unsafe explanation: more than 3 weeks, raised firm (indurated) edges, bleeding, lateral tongue or floor of mouth, and a neck lump.

Tobacco and alcohol are the main risk factors and multiply each other’s effect. Areca nut (in betel quid and paan) is classed as a human carcinogen by IARC (international). Offer stop smoking support (NICE NG209) and alcohol brief advice (NICE PH24).
The specialist will examine, usually biopsy the ulcer, and may scan the neck. NHS England’s Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about the ulcer; takes the neck lump seriously as part of the agenda rather than a throwaway.
Smoking, daily alcohol and paan asked without judgement; the wife’s role; his brother’s illness.
The wife’s worry and “that’s just a gland, isn’t it?” are followed up and lead to the fear underneath.
Idea (denture sore); concern (brother’s mouth and throat cancer, fear of treatment); expectation (gel or mouthwash).
Arranges face-to-face examination to palpate the ulcer and neck; explains the specialist will examine and biopsy.
Denture trauma versus oral cancer; checks whether easing the denture has helped and whether the lump persists.
Duration over 3 weeks, induration, bleeding, neck lump; asks about swallowing, voice, ear pain and weight loss.
States that the ulcer is suspicious and meets the NICE NG12 criteria, without claiming it is cancer.
Suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer sent today (NICE NG12); gel for comfort only.
Offers stop smoking support, alcohol advice and paan cessation respectfully; denture left out meanwhile.
Chase if no contact within a week; same-day contact for heavy bleeding, swallowing or breathing trouble; results reviewed together.

social.t: Betel, paan and areca nut chewing can be a long-standing social and cultural habit. Ask about it routinely and neutrally; many patients do not know it carries a cancer risk.
His brother’s difficult treatment drives his avoidance. His wife is an ally in getting him to appointments.

legal.t: Explain why a suspected cancer referral is being made, what it involves and that it does not mean cancer is confirmed. Patients who are told the reason are more likely to attend.

professional.t: The GP remains responsible for checking the patient is seen. Record the referral, the reason given to the patient and a plan to follow up if he does not hear.
A photo cannot show induration or feel the neck. Arrange examination in person, but do not delay the referral waiting for it.

community.t: NHS Stop Smoking Services; local alcohol support; Macmillan Cancer Support and the Mouth Cancer Foundation for information while he waits.

redFlags: Unexplained oral ulceration for more than 3 weeks: suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer (NICE NG12)
Persistent unexplained neck lump: oral cancer criterion, and laryngeal criterion at 45 and over
Raised, firm edges, bleeding, lateral tongue site; difficulty swallowing, voice change, ear pain, weight loss
psychosocial: Forty years of smoking, daily alcohol and occasional paan
Brother’s head and neck cancer and his experience of treatment
His wife’s concern as a reliable signal
ice: Idea: “It’s the denture rubbing; the lump is just a gland”
Concern: ending up like his brother
Expectation: a mouth gel or mouthwash

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This ulcer has been there six weeks, has firm edges and bleeds, and there’s a lump in your neck. That doesn’t fit with a denture sore, so it needs checking quickly by the head and neck specialists.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A sore from a denture is like a blister from new shoes: once the rubbing stops, it heals. This one hasn’t healed even with the denture out, so we need someone to take a proper look and probably a small sample.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me about your brother, and I understand why you’d want this to be the denture. Getting it checked early is the best way to avoid what he went through.”
management.psychosocial: Respect his pace on smoking, drinking and paan: make one open offer of support and let him choose. Involve his wife if he wants.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to head and neck today (NICE NG12)
Face-to-face examination this week to palpate the ulcer and neck, without delaying the referral
Gel for comfort only; denture out where possible; stop smoking support offered
safetyNet: Ring if no hospital contact within a week
Same-day contact for heavy bleeding, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or a rapidly growing lump

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on knowledge of NICE NG12. They fail by going along with the patient’s explanation, missing the neck lump, or losing him with a lecture. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Prescribes a gel and asks him to return in two weeks if it hasn’t healed.
items.why: The ulcer has already lasted six weeks. It meets the NICE NG12 threshold now. “Management not in line with UK guidance.”
items.fix: State the criterion plainly and send the suspected cancer pathway referral today.

items.fail: Accepts “the lump is just a gland from the ulcer”.
items.why: A persistent unexplained neck lump is its own NICE NG12 criterion, and with the ulcer raises concern for spread.
items.fix: Ask how long it has been there and whether it is changing, and include it in the referral.

items.why: Induration and nodes are felt, not seen. Over-reliance on a remote image is unsafe.
items.fix: Refer now and arrange a face-to-face examination this week; one does not wait for the other.

items.fail: Lectures on smoking, drinking and paan before he feels heard.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s perspective.” Shame about a cultural habit can end engagement.
items.fix: Ask neutrally, thank him for honesty, and make one open offer of support later in the consultation.

items.fail: Never discovers why he wants it to be the denture.
items.why: “Did not explore concerns.” His brother’s cancer is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Use the wife’s worry: “It sounds like she’s worried. What about you?”

items.fail: Says “it’s probably cancer” or, conversely, “I’m sure it’s nothing”.
items.why: Both are poorly calibrated communication and damage trust.
items.fix: “Most mouth ulcers aren’t cancer, but this one needs a proper look, quickly.”
